gospel.d: The worship music of the Black church: call-and-response between lead singer and choir, thick harmonies, Hammond organ; it later fed soul, R&B and rock 'n' roll.

blues.d: Twelve-bar form, blue notes and conversational phrasing; from field hollers to electric Chicago blues, it is the shared ancestor of modern popular music.

delta-blues.d: The raw blues of the Mississippi Delta: slide guitar and gritty vocals; Robert Johnson's recordings became the scripture for every blues that followed.

boogie-woogie.d: A piano blues offshoot: the left hand drives an unbroken eighth-note bass figure that directly foreshadowed the rhythm of rock 'n' roll.

jump-blues.d: Postwar blues handed to big-voiced singers and horn riffs, faster and built for the dance floor; the forerunner of R&B.

chicago-blues.d: Delta blues moved north to Chicago and was amplified through electric guitar, harmonica and a full band, becoming rock 'n' roll's direct teacher.

folk.d: A vernacular tradition built on narrative ballads and acoustic guitar; politicized by the folk revival of the 20th century, it later nourished rock.

country.d: Southern American storytelling with guitar, fiddle and steel guitar, singing of honky-tonks, love and homesickness.

bluegrass.d: High-energy acoustic music from Appalachia: banjo, mandolin, fiddle and high harmony, played at breakneck speed.

honky-tonk.d: Country music for the barroom: electric guitar, piano and drums, with lyrics back on drinking and heartbreak.

country-rock.d: Country melody and harmony dropped into a rock band; Gram Parsons and The Byrds led the way.

outlaw-country.d: 1970s country made outside the Nashville system: rougher, more rock-oriented and more stubbornly individual in spirit.

ragtime.d: Late-19th-century syncopated piano music: a steady bass in the left hand, syncopated melody in the right, the direct forerunner of jazz.

new-orleans-jazz.d: Collective improvisation from New Orleans: trumpet, clarinet and trombone all talking at once, played for funerals and parades alike.

swing.d: Ballroom jazz of the big-band era: a driving rhythm section and call-and-response horn sections; it ruled American pop in the 1930s.

bebop.d: A postwar small-group revolution: fast tempos, complex harmony, improvisation above all, pushing jazz from the ballroom toward art music.

cool-jazz.d: A reaction against bebop: slower, more restrained, focused on arrangement and tone color; the face of West Coast jazz.

hard-bop.d: Bringing the grit of blues and gospel back into jazz, with funkier drums and bass; the breeding ground for soul jazz.

modal-jazz.d: A few modes replace frequent chord changes, letting soloists stretch out over a single harmony for a long time.

free-jazz.d: Fixed harmony and meter are abandoned, pushing collective improvisation to the edge of noise and energy.

jazz-fusion.d: Jazz players plug in: rock beats, funk bass, synthesizers; Miles Davis's Bitches Brew was the watershed.

smooth-jazz.d: The 1980s radio-friendly strain of jazz: synthesizer beds, soft grooves and melodies that never confront the listener.

acid-jazz.d: Jazz samples, funk grooves and house beats stitched together, a product of the London club scene.

nu-jazz.d: From the late 1990s, electronic producers and jazz players collaborated, carrying jazz improvisation into clubs and headphones.

rhythm-and-blues.d: Postwar fusion of jump-blues horns, gospel voices and boogie groove; the common source of soul, funk and rock 'n' roll.

doo-wop.d: Street-corner vocal harmony, either a cappella or lightly backed, with stacked thirds and romantic lyrics at its center.

soul.d: Gospel passion poured into secular love songs, with the voice as absolute lead; the mainstream of Black American music in the 1960s.

motown.d: Detroit's polished take on soul: pop melodies, tight arrangements and factory-style production, built for a crossover market.

funk.d: Accent on the one, bass in charge, drums and guitar chopped into interlocking grooves; James Brown made rhythm itself the star.

psychedelic-soul.d: Soul music meets psychedelic rock, taking in distorted textures, echo, social awareness and experimental arrangements.

philadelphia-soul.d: Philadelphia's sweet soul sound: sweeping strings, Latin percussion and lush arrangements, one of disco's direct ancestors.

quiet-storm.d: Late-1970s slow-jam R&B: romantic, silky and seductive, the soundtrack to late-night radio and the bedroom.

contemporary-rnb.d: R&B after the 1980s: drum machines, synthesizers and sleeker production; Michael Jackson and Whitney Houston took it global.

new-jack-swing.d: A late-1980s R&B offshoot built on swinging drum-machine patterns, choice samples and an unmistakable hip-hop attitude.

neo-soul.d: From the mid-to-late 1990s, bringing live instruments, jazz harmony and hip-hop drums back to soul.

alternative-rnb.d: A 2010s strain of R&B: atmospheric production, electronic textures and an intimate vocal style that blurs genre boundaries.

disco.d: Born in New York's underground dance floors in the 1970s: four-on-the-floor dance music distilled from funk, soul, Philadelphia soul and salsa, reworked by DJs through 12-inch extended mixes. After the 1979 backlash it went underground, only to spawn house and techno.

boogie.d: The lighter offshoot after disco receded: synth bass, looser drums and a stronger R&B flavor.

post-disco.d: The transitional years after 1979: disco's dance-floor DNA broken up into R&B, synth-pop and early electronic music.

hi-nrg.d: Faster and more synthesizer-driven than disco, this was the pumping high-energy sound of 1980s gay dance floors.

italo-disco.d: Italian and European synth disco driven by mechanical drum machines, melodic synthesizers and robotic vocals.

nu-disco.d: A 2000s retro reworking of disco that combines live bass, strings and contemporary dance-music production.
